# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical Reading: "Two Years On" (Varden 24-Month Follow-up and Halden Subset)

This report settles a good deal. On the strictest measure, the gain in output per hour persists at 24 months but is smaller: +8.5% on system logs, +9.8% on timesheets. The "entirely an artifact" claim and the "no decay" claim are both answered well. The weaker parts are:
- **Contamination:** two control offices adopted the treatment's main ingredient. The report does not consider what this does to its estimate of decay.
- **The log measure:** what it counts is unclear, and that affects both the hours figures and the mediation analysis.
- **The mediation:** "confirms" overstates what it can show.
- **Authorship:** the authors are judging critiques of their own earlier work, and the Halden attrition misstatement goes unaddressed.

## 1. Arithmetic check

- **Output per hour at 24 months:** 0.966/0.88 = +9.8% on timesheets, and 0.966/0.89 = +8.5% on logs. Both correct.
- **Halden continuers:** hours fell 13.4% (34.9/40.3 = 0.866), and 96.8/86.6 = +11.8%. Correct.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **"Declined by about a quarter":** 12.5% to 9.8% is a fall of 22%. "About a fifth" is closer.

**Counter-office cost does not reconcile.** Restoring contacts to baseline needs about 1/0.886, or roughly 12.9% more staff, which matches the "12%". But with pay unchanged, 12% more staff for the same output means wage cost per contact rises about 12%, not 9%. The 9% only works if wages are about three-quarters of total cost. Also, 12% more staff restores the number of contacts handled, not presence or waiting times. Matching the old presence would take about 20% more staff (1/0.83).

## 2. Contamination of the control group affects the decay estimate

From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their recurring meetings, and their output per hour rose 4.1%. In effect, they adopted the treatment's main active ingredient. The report presents this as an "unplanned observation" about mechanisms. It does not consider what it does to the main result:

- **Size of the effect.** If two of seven control offices improved by about 4%, the control average rises by about 1.2 points over the later months.
- **What it does to decay.** That alone could account for a substantial part of the fall from 12.5% to 9.8%. Some of the apparent decay may be the control group improving, not the treatment fading.
- **Probable cause.** Control staff knew about the trial, so the audit was plausibly prompted by it.

A sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or their months after month 15, is needed before the fall is attributed to fading. Until then, the decay estimate is an upper bound.

## 3. What the log measure counts is unclear

The logs record "active log-in time on the county's case-management system… time staff are working on cases". Taken literally, that excludes meetings. But the numbers don't fit that reading.

| Group | Change in meeting time | Change in total hours | Change in non-meeting time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated offices | 7.4 → 3.9 hours | −12% | about −3% (30.5 → 29.5 hours) |
| Control offices | roughly flat | roughly flat | roughly flat |

If the logs measured case work only, logged hours should have fallen about 3%, not 11%. Either the logs capture something close to total time, including time logged in during meetings, or the description is wrong. This matters for two reasons:

- **Unrecorded work.** Logs miss work done off the system: email, phone calls and paper. They tighten the timesheet measure but don't fully address unrecorded work.
- **The mediation outcome.** "Output per log-measured hour" means different things depending on what the logs include (see section 4).

## 4. The mediation: "confirms" is too strong

- **A key assumption is untestable.** Randomisation applies to treatment, not to the mediators. As the Limitations section admits, the shares depend on there being no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome. Well-run offices might, for example, both cut meetings and improve output. A registered test makes the result more credible, but it cannot confirm a mechanism that rests on an untestable assumption. "Supports" would be accurate.
- **Office-months are not a larger sample.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds repeated measurements, not independent units. Inference still rests on 14 clusters, the same problem with few clusters that I raised for the nine-month report. A 95% interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 7 v 7 offices.
- **Where did the baseline meeting data come from?** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. This report gives baseline meeting times (7.4 and 7.2 hours). They were presumably reconstructed retrospectively from calendars, which may undercount meetings that were cancelled or deleted. The source should be stated.
- **Simple accounting suggests meetings explain almost everything.** Section 3 above shows non-meeting time fell about 4% relative to control, and output fell about 3.4%. So output per non-meeting hour is roughly unchanged. If meetings produce little output, removing them accounts for nearly the whole per-hour gain, not 47%.
  - This rests on approximate hours levels.
  - It also clarifies what the gain mostly is: unproductive hours removed from the denominator, not people working harder or better.
  - The gap between this simple figure and the model's 47% needs explaining, and may come back to the log measure in section 3.
- **The shares may overlap.** Fewer meetings could also reduce fatigue, so the two pathways may not be separable and additive as Table 2 implies.

## 5. Halden subset

- **More attrition.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded. The nine that did not are a new loss to follow-up, and their outcomes are unknown.
- **One reversion is not a coverage case.** The summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations". But one was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. That is deadline-driven, which the meta-analysis would code as discretionary rather than coverage-bound. Folding it into "coverage" understates the risk in discretionary work.
- **Including the reverters lowers the output figure.** With the three reverters' output at about 88–91, all 14 together come to roughly 95, not 96.8.
- **"Upper bound" is too precise.** The authors rightly call these organisations "survivors twice over". But their figure is biased upward without being a strict bound, because unlogged hours and the lack of a comparison group could push it either way.

## 6. Authorship and unfinished business

R. Okafor, the lead author of the Halden working paper, is a co-author here. The Varden authors are likewise assessing a critique of their own exploratory analysis.

The rebuttals are largely evidence-based. But the report does not acknowledge the most serious finding against Halden: the attrition was misdescribed as preparation-phase withdrawal for scheduling reasons. A follow-up co-authored by the original lead author should correct that record.

## 7. What the report gets right

- **The rebuttal of "entirely an artifact" is decisive.** The 24-month estimate meets the critics' own recommended standards: randomisation, record-based output, stricter hours measurement and long follow-up. It finds +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8).
- **The rebuttal of the meta-analysis on decay is decisive.** All four long-follow-up studies in the meta-analysis were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, confirming what I suspected. The "no decay" claim therefore cannot be sustained.
- **Coverage-bound work is settled for this employer.** The counter arm was ended at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the report now gives this comparison against control, which was missing before.
- **The meeting-audit evidence is presented honestly.** The report frames it with appropriate caution and correctly says the trial cannot separate "reorganisation alone" from "the hours cut forces reorganisation".

## 8. Still missing

- **Cost per case in case-processing work.** With output per employee down 3.4% at full pay, cost per case is up about 3.5%, plus any overtime. It is still not reported for the arm that continued.
- **Confidence intervals** for sick days and resignations.
- **A sensitivity analysis** excluding the contaminated control offices.
- **A clear definition of the log measure.**

## Updated synthesis

**Discretionary (case-processing) work, randomised, at 24 months**
- Output per hour is up about 8.5–10%. This is less than at nine months, but some of the fall may be control contamination rather than fading.
- Output per employee is down about 3%.
- Cost per unit is up a few percent.

**Mechanism**
- Removing recurring meetings is the leading explanation, possibly the dominant one.
- Rest contributes something smaller.
- Part of the gain may be available without cutting hours, through meeting audits. It is untested whether the hours cut is what makes such changes happen and stick.

**Coverage-bound work**
- Output and service fall.
- Maintaining service costs roughly 10% or more per contact.
- The county abandoned the arm.

**Self-selected private pilots**
- Survivors who continued show a gain of about 12% per hour.
- Some organisations reverted, including at least one doing discretionary work.

**Open questions**
- Whether meeting reform alone matches the gain. This needs a trial arm that reorganises without cutting hours.
- Effects beyond 24 months.
- Settings outside the public sector with randomised designs.
